# Terms that file under something other than what they print

Every term below is written so that its sorted position differs from the
position its printed text alone would give it. The order the marks appear in
is deliberately not the order the index must print, and the twin fixture —
this file with every `sort=` attribute removed and nothing else changed —
prints them in a demonstrably different order.

A leading article files under the word that matters:
[The Hague]{.index}.

A name whose first character sorts nowhere near where a reader looks for it:
[Ångström]{.index}.

A number files where it is spoken:
[10 Downing Street]{.index}.

A nobiliary particle is not the surname:
[von Neumann]{.index}.

A surname files ahead of the given name that precedes it:
[Édouard Manet]{.index}.

# One sort key, several marks

The same term marked again, this time with no `sort=` of its own. A sort key
belongs to the entry rather than to the mark that happened to declare it, so
this mark files under `Hague` too — were it to file under its printed text
instead, the index would carry the term twice, in two places, printed
identically: [The Hague]{.index}.

# Sub-entries sort by their own keys

Two sub-entries under one parent, written in the order their printed text
would give them, so the index cannot be right by having left them alone. The
first level of each sort key is empty, which means "file this level under its
own printed text" — only the second level is being redirected.

Turing: []{.index entry="mathematicians!Alan Turing"}
Neumann: []{.index entry="mathematicians!von Neumann"}
